newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Trade body sees record EU grain crop.
newsitem.headline: Trade body sees record EU grain crop.

text.p: The European Union grain trade group forecast a record European Union crop of 201 million tonnes on Friday, surging 15 percent from last year's harvest after farmers expanded plantings and favourable weather helped to boost yields.

COCERAL, the European grain trade association, raised its forecast for grain production in the 15 member states from 198.5 million in September after members reported higher wheat and maize crop figures.
The previous record was in 1991 when the EU produced 182.6 million tonnes. The figure includes Swedish, Finnish and Austria output although they only joined the EU in 1995.

Farmers took advantage of high world prices last year and an easing of EU planting restrictions to expand the cereals area by five percent while yields shot up nearly 10 percent compared with last year's drought damaged crop.
But a lot of the increase is in poor quality wheat which will have to be exported with the aid of subsidies to enable the EU to find buyers at lower world market levels.
"This will annoy the Americans because it competes with their maize exports," a trade source said.

U.S. Department of Agriculture officials warned the EU's executive Commission during talks in Brussels this week against raising wheat export subsidies and renewing the grain subsidy war of the late 1980s and early 1990s.
The European Commission, which is anxious to avoid a renewed grain trade row with Washington, has said that that figures provided by member states have been over-estimated.
In its latest forecast, COCERAL put the maize harvest, which is not yet complete, 14 percent higher than last year at 33.3 million tonnes. Maize is used mainly to feed farm animals.

Bread-making wheat is seen 12 percent higher at 90.2 million tonnes, barley 19 percent up at 52.3 million and durum wheat, used for pasta and biscuits, is seen jumping 34 percent to 7.6 million tonnes.
The balance is made up of rye, sorghum, oats and other grains used to feed animals.
